<explanation>
1. Identify the project type and purpose
   - This is a modular Swift server framework (Hummingbird). It is not a monolithic full-stack application but a library/framework built on top of SwiftNIO to provide HTTP server functionality, routing, middleware, TLS, HTTP/2, codable support, testing, and benchmarks.
   - The README confirms it is a “lightweight, flexible modern web application framework” with built-in extensions (router, TLS, HTTP/2, testing) and a minimal core.

2. Analyze the file structure
   - Top-level directories:
     • Sources: multiple modules: Hummingbird (high-level API), HummingbirdCore (NIO integration), HummingbirdHTTP2, HummingbirdTLS, HummingbirdRouter, HummingbirdTesting, PerformanceTest  
     • Tests: unit tests for each module  
     • Benchmarks: performance tests for routing  
     • docker, scripts: environment setup and CI scripts  
   - Patterns:
     • Layered architecture: Application → Router → Middleware → Core HTTP server → NIO  
     • Extension modules plugged into the core (router, HTTP/2, TLS)  
     • Middleware pipeline pattern  
     • Adapter pattern for storage drivers  

3. Examine the README for additional insights
   - The user code instantiates a Router, configures routes, creates an Application with address configuration, and runs runService()  
   - It describes built-in and external extensions, highlighting the plug-in architecture  

4. How to create the system design diagram
   a. Main components:
      1. Client (browser/HTTP client)  
      2. Network/TLS Layer (HummingbirdTLS module + SwiftNIO TLS handlers)  
      3. Transport Layer (SwiftNIO HTTP/1 and HTTP/2 channel handlers – HummingbirdCore & HummingbirdHTTP2)  
      4. Core Server (HummingbirdCore.Server)  
      5. Middleware Pipeline (Hummingbird.Middleware)  
      6. Router (HummingbirdRouter or Hummingbird.Router)  
      7. Handlers/User Application Code (routes defined by user)  
      8. Coders (Hummingbird.Codable for JSON, URL-encoded forms)  
      9. Storage (Hummingbird.Storage PersistDriver adapters)  
     10. Utilities (logging, metrics, date cache, etc.)  
   b. Relationships & interactions:
      - Client → Network/TLS Layer: encrypted/unencrypted TCP connection  
      - Network/TLS → Transport: incoming bytes framed as HTTP/1 or HTTP/2 messages  
      - Transport → Core Server: produces Request objects  
      - Core Server → Middleware Pipeline: each middleware processes Request/Response  
      - Middleware → Router: routes request to matching handler  
      - Router → Handler: user-provided code returns a response body or model  
      - Handler → Coders: if return type is Codable, serialize to JSON or form  
      - Response travels back up: Router → Middleware → Core → Transport → Client  
      - Storage drivers invoked by handlers or middleware as needed  
   c. Architectural patterns/design principles:
      - Layered architecture (network → transport → application)  
      - Middleware pipeline (chain of responsibility)  
      - Inversion of Control (user code plugs into framework)  
      - Modular extensibility (each extension is a separate Swift package/module)  
      - Adapter pattern (storage drivers, HTTP2, TLS)  
   d. Relevant technologies/frameworks/libraries:
      - SwiftNIO (networking, event loop)  
      - Swift Concurrency (async/await)  
      - Swift Codable system  
      - Trie-based router (Hummingbird.Router/TrieRouter)  
      - TLS (NIOTLS)  
      - HTTP/2 state machine  

5. Guidelines for tailoring the diagram
   - Since this is a server framework library:
     • Emphasize the core framework layers rather than a single deployed service  
     • Show extension modules branching off the core (e.g., HTTP2, TLS, RouterBuilder)  
     • Highlight the plugin points (middleware, router, storage)  
     • You may show sample user application at the top that invokes the Application API  

6. Diagram elements to include
   - Clear labels for each layer and module (e.g., “HummingbirdCore.Server”, “MiddlewareGroup”, “TrieRouter”)  
   - Directional arrows showing data/request flow from client → framework → handlers → client  
   - Color-coding or distinct shapes:
     • Blue rectangles for core modules  
     • Green for extension modules  
     • Yellow cylinder for storage adapters  
     • Cloud icon for external client  
   - Optional legend for shapes/colors  

7. Detailed breakdown for the diagram
   - Layer 1: Client (cloud icon)  
   - Layer 2: Network/TLS  
     • HummingbirdTLS.TLSChannel (encrypt/decrypt)  
   - Layer 3: Transport  
     • HummingbirdHTTP2.HTTP2Channel & HummingbirdCore.Server HTTP1Channel  
   - Layer 4: Core Server  
     • HummingbirdCore.ServerBuilder → RequestResponder  
   - Layer 5: Middleware  
     • LogRequestMiddleware → CORSMiddleware → FileMiddleware → MetricsMiddleware → TracingMiddleware  
   - Layer 6: Router  
     • Hummingbird.Router / HummingbirdRouter.RouterBuilder / TrieRouter  
   - Layer 7: Handlers  
     • User-defined GET /hello, etc.  
   - Layer 8: Codable  
     • JSONCoding & URLEncodedFormEncoder/Decoder  
   - Layer 9: Storage  
     • MemoryPersistDriver or custom PersistDriver  
   - Layer 10: Utils (ByteBuffer+foundation, DateCache, HexDigest)  

By following these guidelines and tailoring each box/arrow to the actual module names and data flows, you will produce a detailed, accurate system design diagram reflecting Hummingbird’s architecture. Ensure each component is labeled, arrows show flow, and colors differentiate layers and extensions.
